candidates.evidence: The ASRM opinion's public and affected-patient claims can be traced to five named studies. Barton et al. surveyed 1,049 US adults: 47.8% supported posthumous retrieval from men and 42.7% from women; among supporters, 69.8% considered prior consent necessary (PMID 22763100). Hans surveyed 2,064 US adults by random-digit dialing; among respondents aged 18-44, 70% of men and 58% of women wanted a surviving spouse to be able to use their gametes after death (PMID 25134070). Pastuszak et al. reviewed signed sperm-bank choices from 364 patients and found 85.9% consented to post-mortem use, with especially high consent among partnered men (PMID 23315967). Nakhuda et al. surveyed 106 couples seeking fertility treatment; about 78% would permit posthumous assisted reproduction, with couple-level concordance about 75% (PMID 21982730). Cote et al. examined signed forms from 498 IVF users; 73.5% of men and 61.8% of women agreed to leave cryopreserved embryos to their partners for reproductive use after death (PMID 25217872). Together these directly ground both orientations in the public pool: strong salience of prior consent and substantial, non-universal willingness to authorize surviving-partner use.
